item.title: Tiyan High School passes sanitation inspection
item.description: The Tiyan High School campus, which has been closed for repairs since August, passed a sanitation inspection conducted by the Department of Public Health and Social Services. item.content:encoded:
The Tiyan High School campus, which has been closed for repairs since August, passed a sanitation inspection conducted by the Department of Public Health and Social Services.

Guam Department of Education spokesperson Damen Michael Borja said details on the return to campus are still in the planning phase. The department will hold meetings with students, parents and others before making final decisions.

The campus housed students from both Tiyan and Simon Sanchez High Schools when classes began in August, but the facility was closed after failing a sanitation inspection. Eventually, students from Simon Sanchez were sent to Okkodo High School, and students from Tiyan were sent to George Washington High School.

All four schools are conducting split sessions.

Borja said the Tiyan inspection was conducted Tuesday morning and involved all areas except those cordoned off for renovations.

item.title: Guam schools lose WASC accreditation due to outstanding purchase order payment
item.description: Several Guam schools were recently notified that their accreditation was terminated, effective immediately, by the Western Association of Schools and Colleges. The Guam Department of Education did not name the schools that were involved and did not say how many had their accreditation terminated.
item.content:encoded:
Several Guam schools were recently notified that their accreditation was terminated, effective immediately, by the Western Association of Schools and Colleges.

The Guam Department of Education did not name the schools that were involved and did not say how many had their accreditation terminated.

GDOE spokesperson Damen Michael Borja said the termination stems from an outstanding purchase order payment from School Year 2024–2025 that was not processed at the time.

Borja said the department has since addressed the outstanding payment, which was completed Monday.

He said the department is currently awaiting confirmation from WASC regarding accreditation status.

Borja said remains committed to working collaboratively with WASC and will continue efforts to secure the required WASC membership for School Year 2026–2027.

item.title: Community fishing locker installed in Hagåtña Mayor’s Office
item.description: The Department of Agriculture’s Division of Aquatic and Wildlife Resources, or DAWR, and the Hagåtña Mayor’s Office have installed a community fishing locker at the Hagåtña Mayor’s Office. The gear is available to all Guam residents with a valid form of identification. There is no age restriction, and the equipment includes reels sized for children.
item.content:encoded:
The Department of Agriculture’s Division of Aquatic and Wildlife Resources, or DAWR, and the Hagåtña Mayor’s Office have installed a community fishing locker at the Hagåtña Mayor’s Office.

The gear is available to all Guam residents with a valid form of identification. There is no age restriction, and the equipment includes reels sized for children.

The locker has six rod-and-reel combinations in varying sizes, as well as tackle boxes and fishing tackle.

Adults may borrow equipment for themselves or on behalf of a child or guardian.

Borrowers must provide valid identification, complete a Fishing Locker Checkout Form, and sign a participant agreement. After use, the equipment must be returned to the Hagåtña Mayor’s Office for inspection.

DAWR also offers fishing clinics by appointment for community members interested in hands-on fishing instruction.

The Community Fishing Locker was funded through a grant from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Office of Conservation Investment. DAWR says the program aims to make recreational fishing more accessible while encouraging responsible fishing and stewardship of Guam’s aquatic resources.

item.content:encoded:
Eva Marie Saint, who starred in Elia Kazan's 1954 On the Waterfront and Alfred Hitchcock's 1959 North by Northwest, died Tuesday at 102 years old.

Saint grew up in Albany and Delmar, New York. She was a delicate, porcelain beauty. She attended the Actors Studio in New York, performed on Broadway and did live television in the late 1940s. But Saint didn't do a film until she was almost 30, after director Elia Kazan suggested she screen test with a guy named Marlon Brando. They did a scene from On the Waterfront in which Saint is supposed to keep Brando out of her house.

In 2000, Saint told WHYY's Fresh Air , "I don't know what happened, but ... [Brando] came in the living room. We were dancing, we were laughing, I was crying. He was taking my skirt and ... whipping it around, and the sparks flew. And Kazan saw that. And suddenly I was in On the Waterfront ."

In that film, Saint plays Edie, a Catholic schoolgirl who finds herself in the middle of union corruption in Hoboken, N.J. When her longshoreman brother is murdered, Edie wants justice. Saint won an Oscar for performance.

Five years after playing the chaste heroine Edie, Saint played a femme fatale opposite Cary Grant in Alfred Hitchcock's North by Northwest. But Saint was no femme fatale off the screen. After marrying director Jeffrey Hayden in 1951, she limited her roles to devote more time to her children. She went back to TV in the '70s, and won an Emmy in 1990 for the miniseries People Like Us.

item.title: Cornell names former acting U.S. attorney general to review rape case
item.description: Cornell University named Sally Yates, a former acting U.S. attorney general and career federal prosecutor, as head of an independent internal review into how the school handled a former student's rape allegations. The announcement comes as the school continues to face outrage on campus and nationally after a former student filed a civil lawsuit alleging she was drugged and gang raped in 2024. The
item.content:encoded:
Cornell University named Sally Yates, a former acting U.S. attorney general and career federal prosecutor, as head of an independent internal review into how the school handled a former student's rape allegations.

The announcement comes as the school continues to face outrage on campus and nationally after a former student filed a civil lawsuit alleging she was drugged and gang raped in 2024. The woman, identified in the suit as Jane Doe, also alleged failings by the school in how it handled her complaint and the aftermath.

Yates, a partner at King & Spalding who served as the U.S. deputy attorney general under President Barack Obama, was picked by the newly formed Special Committee of the Cornell University Board of Trustees. She will also examine the school's policies related to how it "prevents and responds to sexual harassment, sexual assault and related misconduct on campus," the school announced Tuesday .

"Sally Yates brings extraordinary experience, independence and judgment to this work," said Anne Meinig Smalling, chair of the special committee, in the school's announcement. "The questions raised by the Jane Doe matter warrant a rigorous examination of Cornell's response to that case, but our responsibility is broader. We have asked Ms. Yates and her team to examine Cornell's overall approach to preventing and responding to sexual misconduct, identify where we are doing things well and where we can do better, and recommend changes that will help make our community safer."

Doe filed her lawsuit in mid-September. In it, Doe alleges that seven men drugged and assaulted her for several hours in October 2024 at their Chi Phi fraternity house on campus. No criminal charges were ever filed against the men. Those named in the lawsuit have denied all wrongdoing. Cornell University is also named as a defendant in Doe's suit.

The university has maintained that Cornell University Police investigated the case thoroughly and that the school held its own Title IX investigation, which resulted in suspensions and expulsions.

But in the weeks that have followed the lawsuit's filing, students have protested the university's response to the case. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed state Attorney General Letitia James to lead a criminal investigation into the rape case, after sharp criticism of its handling by campus police and the local prosecutor, Matthew Van Houten. The case also has renewed national conversations over consent and sexual assault on college campuses.

item.title: France's police fire tear gas and water cannons as school protests sweep the country
item.description: PARIS — Police fired tear gas to control crowds in Paris and elsewhere in France on Tuesday as more than a quarter of a million people rallied nationwide to support high school students demanding more education funding, according to government figures. item.content:encoded:
PARIS — Police fired tear gas to control crowds in Paris and elsewhere in France on Tuesday as more than a quarter of a million people rallied nationwide to support high school students demanding more education funding, according to government figures. The protests increased pressure on the administration of outgoing President Emmanuel Macron.

As pupils blockaded high schools, large crowds waving flags and placards gathered in Marseille, Strasbourg and other cities. The demonstrations showed how protests that began at a high school in the Paris region in mid-September have grown into a nationwide movement — the latest of many that have marked Macron's nearly decade-long tenure.

"We need to listen to them," said Léa Monimart, an adult demonstrator in the northern city of Lille. "They are 17 years old; they are not completely clueless, and they know what they are talking about. It's important to show that there are adults who support them."

The Interior Ministry estimated that 266,000 people took part in demonstrations across the country on Tuesday, including 56,000 in Paris, where small groups of protesters clashed with riot officers at a city square at the end of a largely peaceful march.

Nearly 500 people were detained Tuesday, the ministry said. The widespread use of arrests, tear gas and riot-control weapons against teenagers is fueling defiance and angering some parents and teachers. Some student groups called for new protests Thursday.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said the police response had been proportionate in "almost all cases" and that the protests had at times turned into riots, requiring police intervention.

French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said the government and school leaders must listen to students' concerns and find solutions.

Questioned in parliament on Tuesday about the protest movement, Lecornu denounced "ultra violence" threatening schools. Responding to criticism of police tactics, he pledged that any "accidents" would be investigated and described allegations that the police are racist as a "lie."

More than two weeks of class boycotts and school blockades, and policing that has led to more than 6,500 arrests, mostly of minors, have become a flashpoint in the early days of the presidential election campaign.

Felix Barney, a university student, described the police response as disproportionate, saying it doesn't make "any sense to hit minors."

"Riot police, batons, rubber bullets, tear gas," said Aurélien Le Coq, a lawmaker with the far-left France Unbowed party. Its presidential candidate is strongly backing the protests.

The violence is "absolutely unbearable," Le Coq said.

Nuñez defended police tactics despite a growing number of severe injuries blamed on officers' riot-control weapons. In the latest case, a 15-year-old boy lost a hand Monday in an incident involving a police stun grenade. He said 715 officers had been injured.

The teenage protesters have struck a chord amid widespread discontent in France. Frustrations extend beyond immediate difficulties, such as fuel prices that have soared because of the Iran war, to broader concerns about constraints on public spending, rising poverty and wealth inequality under Macron, who can't run for a third consecutive term.

Against that backdrop, pupils' complaints that education funding shortfalls are endangering their futures have found a sympathetic audience.

"You say 'young people are the future,' so listen to them," read a handwritten placard attached to a metal barrier outside a Paris school.

At the Hélène Boucher lycée, or high school, in Paris' 20th district, protesters tipped over trash cans and bicycles onto their sides to create a makeshift barricade.

Like hundreds of others around the country, the school was closed. Authorities began shutting schools last week to take some steam out of the demonstrations after widespread damage to schools and mounting injuries among staff, students and police. Classes were totally or partially suspended on Tuesday at 891 schools, according to the Education Ministry.

Facing accusations that it was ignoring protesters, the ministry launched an online portal inviting high school students to anonymously describe the difficulties they face at school and the changes they want to see.

At Hélène Boucher, parents and other adults positioned themselves on Tuesday between protesters and police keeping watch.

"They are our children. Teachers, parents, federations, we all share the same goal: the protection of children's rights, and it is a legitimate right to demonstrate and to make demands," said Emilia Sichili Suriam, who is a member of an association of parents.

Demonstrators have voiced a range of grievances, often centering on a lack of resources and opportunities for students in disadvantaged schools, despite the promise of France's national motto: "Liberty, Equality, Fraternity."

Students have drawn attention to rundown classrooms that lack basics such as desks and chairs, become sweltering in summer without air conditioning and, in some cases, are infested with rats. Other common complaints include staff shortages and exhausting workloads. French high school students' compulsory classroom hours are among the highest in Europe.

Suzanne Nijdam, president of the federation of student associations, vowed that demonstrations would continue until authorities address the complaints.

"So, we really need to act now, and it's in the government's hands, to see these demands through to the end," she said. "It's a matter of political priority, a matter of prioritizing the youth and the future of our country."

Neighboring Belgium is also seeing student protests. More than 30 were arrested Tuesday and several police injured in the eastern city of Liege, and smaller protests were held in Brussels and other cities.

item.title: 'Here I am, my full, authentic self': Murray Hill charts his own course in 'Showbiz!'
item.description: Murray Hill calls himself "Mr. Showbiz." In addition to playing Fred Rococo in the HBO series, Somebody Somewhere , Hill hosted drag king shows, queer cabarets and comedy shows — and he performs his own act. "I started producing and creating shows because this is my mantra … if you don't see yourself represented, go out and represent yourself," Hill says.
item.content:encoded:
Murray Hill calls himself "Mr. Showbiz." In addition to playing Fred Rococo in the HBO series, Somebody Somewhere , Hill hosted drag king shows, queer cabarets and comedy shows — and he performs his own act.

"I started producing and creating shows because this is my mantra … if you don't see yourself represented, go out and represent yourself," Hill says.

Hill grew up in New England, raised by a conservative Catholic mother who wanted an obedient, feminine daughter, and a father who, he says, largely ignored him.

"It was just incongruous from day one," he says. "And so I left a place where I was not welcome, or cared for or seen, and went to college. But it wasn't until I got to New York and found my people and the city, that I actually was like, 'Oh, I can actually be this person.'"

Initially, "Murray Hill" was a stage persona, but over time the name came to represent who he really is: "Today, here I am, my full, authentic self, and I feel like this is who I was when I was born," Hill says.

He says he spent years separating himself from his traumatic childhood, but more recently, Hill felt a need to acknowledge and stop suppressing those painful memories. His new memoir is Showbiz! My Life as a Middle-Aged Man.

"The book started off as me wanting to do service for the community and for the trans kids, because a lot of the feedback that I received from being Fred Rococo was from parents that have trans kids, community members [who said], 'You were such a good role model, you showed my child that you can have a full career,'" Hill says. "I felt a little disingenuous in that the world and the fans and my friends and my people have only seen the end result of the struggle."

The persona of Murray Hill has like two lanes — one is to take up space to represent a community and a gender that hasn't had equal representation at all within the queer community and within society — still the same today. So that's the public piece to it, but the personal piece of this, Terry, is that I always felt like I was a boy. I grew up thinking I was the tomboy. And then society and my family is like, no, you're a girl. And then in, I think, fourth grade, I dressed up like Schneider from One Day at a Time . And nobody batted an eye. I showed up to school with a mustache, cigarettes rolled in my hair, the tool belt, and everything. But that didn't feel like drag to me.

On his real friendship with Bridget Everett , which became the basis of Somebody Somewhere

Fred is this kind of paternal figure and is creating community and inviting people into it and propping them up. Bridget, we were bosom buddies, friends, for a long time. And we both were kind of othered in very different ways. So she got to New York and wanted to be in the theater community and a singer like a traditional theater singer. And I was in the queer community. But when we found each other, we related on [being misfits] and we instantly bonded. And the gay community took her in, Terry, with wide open arms. … But the gay community has a huge history of loving and supporting strong, powerful women with a voice. So Bridget became part of this misfit choir practice community, [and] that's the very basis of Somebody Somewhere . So a lot of people said that me and Jeff [Hiller] and Bridget were so real on the show, that the show was so authentic.

On the difference between himself and the character he played in Somebody Somewhere

Fred Rococo is me dialed down to like a 2, with 10 being the highest. I have a very big personality … Fred was more calm than I am, but what we did share was enormous heart and wanting to connect with people through our heart and not how we identify and not through our circumstances. Fred is like me with bad purple clothing, no mustache, and kind of subtle. ...

Before Somebody Somewhere came out, this was like the week before, I went to see her in hospice. And the woman that has taken up so much space in my mind and in my life as being essentially a monster was helpless, vulnerable … So she felt like a completely different person. And the way that I felt about her in that room was how I feel about every single other person in my life, empathy. It wasn't the angry mother or the abusive person … I saw a woman that has been so tough as nails her entire life, finally, in the last few days, let her guard down. And it was incredibly profound. In that moment, I was sitting next to her, holding her hand and I said to myself, "I forgive you."

It's not even that she did the best that she could — she could have done better, for sure. That's not an excuse … but hurt people hurt people.

On not feeling represented in '80s drag culture

I looked around and I was like, "Holy crap, there's no lesbians here. There's no drag kings here. There's no butches." It was all drag queens and gay men. So I really didn't see anybody like me. So that's when the epiphany was: What is on the other side of this gender spectrum? That's where I need to go. … A day later, I went and looked at a magazine … and there was a listing for a drag king pageant at the Hershey Bar. So I had my big Pentax camera with a huge flash and I told the door person I was from The Village Voice and that I was reporting on the pageant and they let me in.

It wasn't campy like the drag queens in Boston or Wigstock that I had photographed. It didn't have the humor. … It was almost very serious. It was very masculine. It was almost more about passing. I was mesmerized by it, and I took these photos from these early pageants of these drag kings, and my mind was working overtime. … So I really saw a window there. … [With] '70s performance art, the major motto was "the personal is political," so I jumped on the other side of the camera, and I became what I did not see.

On feeling the impact of Trump's anti-trans rhetoric

I've been around for a while. It's never been great for us, and it's never great for the queer community. I think there was a little bit of hope that came in with the Obama years and with Biden. But since then, it has gone completely reverse to a point that's so absurd and so hateful and so divisive and cruel that I can't help but feel it in my own life, but I also feel very protective of the young kids who grew up with Obama that didn't think that they were degenerates and weren't stripped of basic human rights constantly, like every day there's something else. So I feel for these kids that we finally got to a place where we were going to live [and] let live, and then also have policies and laws that would ensure equal rights. And now that's gone. So it's mind blowing to me from a societal perspective and from a personal. I definitely feel on a daily basis that there is a target on my back.

[But] it doesn't impact how I present. ... I'm not gonna hide and I'm gonna bow down. I am gonna take up space, represent myself and the community and show people … that I am just like you. Because I do feel, Terry, that it's my social responsibility to be out there even more. And that's the message: We're here, we're not going anywhere, and there's nothing to be afraid of, people.

Anna Bauman and Nico Gonzalez Wisler produced and edited this interview for broadcast. Bridget Bentz, Molly Seavy-Nesper and Beth Novey adapted it for the web.
